analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicaid, Medicare, and private insurers to cover annual lung cancer screening without prior authorization or cost-sharing.
analysis.headline: Introduced with bipartisan backing from a New York Democrat and 9 cosponsors, the bill sat in a House subcommittee for 18 months and never received a committee or floor vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require Medicaid to cover annual lung cancer screening for people the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommends it for, with no copays and no prior-approval requirement from the plan. It would also bar Medicare Advantage plans and private insurers from requiring prior approval for these screenings, and expand Medicaid coverage of smoking-cessation counseling and medication to all enrollees instead of just pregnant women. It additionally funds a federal outreach campaign and orders a study of groups the screening guidelines miss, such as firefighters, veterans, and women under 50.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicaid enrollees who smoke or otherwise face high lung cancer risk — a group that skews toward lower incomes — gain a guaranteed annual screening with no copay and no prior-approval hurdle, including if they are in a managed care plan. Medicare beneficiaries and people with private or employer insurance gain protection against plans delaying or denying the screening through prior authorization. All Medicaid enrollees gain coverage of quit-smoking counseling and medication, which today only pregnant women are guaranteed. People whose lung cancer is caught earlier through screening avoid the much worse odds of late-stage diagnosis.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Smokers and low-income patients at high risk

how_it_helps.text: Requires state Medicaid programs to cover annual lung cancer screening — following U.S. Preventive Services Task Force guidelines — with no cost sharing and regardless of prior authorization, including for enrollees in Medicaid managed care plans.

Bars Medicare Advantage plans and private group and individual health plans from imposing any prior-authorization requirement on a recommended annual lung cancer screening, so plans cannot delay or gatekeep the test.

Expands Medicaid coverage of tobacco-cessation counseling and medication from pregnant women only to all enrollees, and prohibits prior authorization for that coverage — lung cancer's main cause, smoking, hits Medicaid populations hardest.

Authorizes $10 million per year for fiscal 2023 through 2027 for a Health and Human Services outreach campaign about who should be screened, and directs a Government Accountability Office study of groups missed by current guidelines, such as firefighters, veterans, and women under 50.

analysis.who_pays: Federal and state governments pay for the additional Medicaid screenings and cessation treatment, with states bearing the largest new share since Congress is mandating coverage without new state funding. Private insurers and the employers who buy their plans absorb the cost of screenings paid without utilization controls, which tends to show up in premiums. Insurers and Medicaid managed care plans also lose a cost-control tool — prior authorization — for this service. A secondary cost is medical: screening can flag nodules that turn out to be harmless, sending some patients for follow-up scans and procedures they did not need.
analysis.who_pays_short: States, Medicaid plans, and private insurers

drawbacks.text: The Medicaid provisions are an unfunded mandate: states must add screening and quit-smoking coverage to their plans, and in states where legislation is required the bill merely delays the deadline rather than paying the bill — costs land on state budgets at a time when states are already covering enrollees the pandemic era added.

No cost estimate appears in the record, so no one knows the price for states, Medicare, or private premiums; removing prior authorization entirely raises utilization with no utilization management even for borderline cases.

Lung cancer screening produces false positives — low-dose CT scans flag nodules that are not cancer — so guaranteed screening without prior authorization means more follow-up scans, biopsies, and anxiety for some patients who never had cancer. The bill pairs screening with an outreach campaign, which would amplify this effect.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits run to a population that loses disproportionately to lung cancer — current and former smokers, disproportionately lower-income — and the tools are the ones with the strongest evidence: early detection and quitting smoking. The costs are real but narrow: some added state Medicaid spending, somewhat higher private claims without a utilization check, and a stream of false-positive follow-ups. The honest weakness is design, not intent: no funding accompanies the state mandate, and no cost estimate was ever produced, so lawmakers would have been voting without knowing the price. Still, a guarantee that a recommended cancer screening cannot be delayed for paperwork reasons is a modest, targeted change, and the bill's death without so much as a committee vote left the prior-approval hurdles in place.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to two House committees and then to a health subcommittee, where it sat for the rest of the Congress and was never brought up for a vote.

narrative.text: Representative Brian Higgins of New York introduced the bill on June 22, 2023, joined from the start by a Republican, Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania, and a Democrat, Kathy Castor of Florida.
The same day, the House referred it to two committees with jurisdiction — Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means — meaning both would have to act before the bill could move.

It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee on June 23, 2023, and again on December 17, 2024, near the end of the Congress; no hearing, markup, or vote ever appears in the action history.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, without the bill ever reaching a floor vote; it cleared a total of zero of the two committees it was assigned to.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and Medicaid managed care plans keep their ability to require prior authorization before approving a lung cancer screening, and state budgets avoid the cost of the new Medicaid coverage mandates. Americans at high risk of lung cancer remain subject to whatever approval hurdles their particular plan imposes.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so the partisan shape of the chamber never got tested; what is known is sponsorship: 7 of 216 House Democrats and 2 of 226 House Republicans signed on, led by a Democrat with a Republican original cosponsor.

industries.note: The bill strips their ability to require prior authorization for a recommended lung cancer screening, meaning more claims paid with no utilization review. Their savings from gating access run directly against patients' access to the test.

They would be contractually required to cover screening and smoking-cessation treatment without prior authorization — losing a cost-control lever — but they would also be paid for each additional screening and treatment delivered. Their gatekeeping interest conflicts with the enrollee's interest in getting screened promptly.

States would bear the cost of guaranteeing screening and cessation coverage for all Medicaid enrollees, an obligation Congress imposed without federal funding attached. Some states would need to pass legislation to comply.

Making quit-smoking counseling and medication available to every Medicaid enrollee attacks the companies' customer base at its most vulnerable point. Anything that increases cessation reduces cigarette sales.

Guaranteed annual screening without prior authorization means more paid low-dose CT scans and more early-stage cancers detected and treated. Their financial interest here lines up with patients getting screened.
